content: The systematic review identified three cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) conducted in Eswatini, Namibia, and Zambia. These studies aimed to evaluate the impact of reactive drug administration (RDA), with reactive case detection and treatment (RACDT) serving as the comparator. However, since RDA is hypothesized to be a more effective strategy than RACDT, no definitive conclusions could be drawn from these studies regarding the effectiveness of RACDT. Two non-randomized studies (NRSs) from Brazil and Zambia reported outcomes among individuals receiving the intervention but did not assess its impact at the community level. Data from 3,926 participants in one study and 215,146 participants in three studies were analyzed. The evidence regarding the effect of RACDT on the incidence of clinical malaria is highly uncertain due to very serious indirectness and serious imprecision. The difference in clinical malaria incidence was estimated at 12 per 1,000 (95% CI: 1 fewer to 17 more), but the certainty of this evidence is very low. Regarding parasitemia prevalence, data from two studies showed a reduction of 3 percentage points at 30, 60, and 180 days in RACD households compared to control households. However, in one study, parasitemia reductions of 1 percentage point at 30 and 90 days were observed in RACD households, but no control households were included. The evidence on the effect of RACDT on parasite prevalence among participants is very uncertain due to serious risk of bias and inconsistency. Adverse events (AEs) were reported in three randomized controlled trials (RCTs). However, AEs were typically only actively solicited from the RDA arm and not from the RACD arm. Among 1,775 individuals treated with dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DP) in the RDA arm, 9% experienced mild AEs, all of which resolved. No AEs were reported in the RACD arm. In another study, 8% of 1,776 participants receiving RDA with DP experienced AEs, with 54 rated as mild and 14 as moderate. The evidence on the effect of RACDT on adverse events is very uncertain due to very serious risk of bias, serious indirectness, and very serious imprecision. The systematic review also identified two cRCTs evaluating reactive indoor residual spraying (RIRS) in Namibia and South Africa. The Namibian study used a 2x2 factorial design to compare RACDT alone, RDA alone, RACDT plus RIRS, and RDA plus RIRS. The South African study was a non-inferiority trial comparing RIRS to standard IRS, which covered one-third of households in defined priority areas. RIRS was associated with a significant reduction in malaria prevalence (risk difference [RD]: -27 per 1,000 persons; 95% CI: -35 to -8 per 1,000 persons; high-certainty evidence). However, its effect on the incidence of clinical malaria varied, with moderate-certainty evidence suggesting it may make little or no difference (RD: -14 per 1,000 person-years; 95% CI: -32 to 4 per 1,000 person-years). RIRS resulted in little to no difference in reported adverse events (RD: 2 per 1,000 persons; 95% CI: -2 to 1 per 1,000 persons; high-certainty evidence) or serious adverse events (deaths). One study reported 23 adverse events among 18 participants receiving reactive IRS, but none were considered related to IRS. In another study comparing reactive IRS to standard IRS over two years, 9 malaria-related deaths were reported in the reactive IRS arm out of a population of 204,237, compared to 12 deaths in the standard IRS arm out of a population of 189,150. The evidence on adverse events related to RIRS is limited and uncertain due to serious indirectness and imprecision.
